name: Geosmin
fact: Humans detect geosmin at around 5 parts per trillion, a more sensitive threshold than a shark has for blood. It is made by soil bacteria, and we are apparently built to notice them.

name: cis-3-Hexen-1-ol
fact: Known as leaf alcohol. Plants release it within seconds of tissue damage. The smell of cut grass is a wound response, chemically a scream.

name: 2-Acetyl-1-pyrroline
fact: Popcorn, jasmine rice and bread crust smell related because they are literally the same molecule. Pandan leaves make it too.

name: Vanillin
fact: Ageing paper degrades into vanillin and other aromatics, which is a large part of why old libraries smell sweet.

name: Ethylvanillin
fact: Roughly three times stronger than vanillin, and not found in vanilla at all. It is a purely synthetic exaggeration of the note.

name: Eugenol
fact: The dentist smell. Eugenol is mildly anaesthetic, which is why clove oil was a toothache remedy long before it was a flavouring.

name: D-Limonene
fact: The spray you see when you bend orange peel is mostly limonene. Its mirror image smells of turpentine and pine instead.

name: Linalool
fact: One of the most widely distributed scent molecules in the plant kingdom, and one of the most common ingredients in soap.

name: Furaneol
fact: Also called strawberry furanone. At high concentration it smells burnt and caramel; dilute it and it turns into ripe fruit.

name: β-Damascenone
fact: Present in rose oil at well under a tenth of a percent, yet it contributes more to the smell of a rose than almost anything else in the bottle.

name: Indole
fact: Concentrated it is unmistakably faecal. Diluted it becomes the warm, almost narcotic body of jasmine. Same molecule, opposite verdict.

name: Skatole
fact: Its name comes from the Greek for dung. It is nonetheless used in trace amounts in perfumery and in vanilla and strawberry flavourings.

name: 2-Isobutyl-3-methoxypyrazine
fact: One of the most potent odorants known. A single drop dispersed in an Olympic swimming pool would still be detectable.

name: 2-Isopropyl-3-methoxypyrazine
fact: The compound behind ladybird taint, a handful of beetles harvested with the grapes is enough to ruin a tank of wine.

name: Diacetyl
fact: The butter note in artificial butter flavouring. Inhaling it industrially causes a lung disease nicknamed popcorn worker's lung.

name: Acetoin
fact: The precursor to diacetyl, and softer than it. The difference between cream and butter in flavour terms.

name: Isoamyl acetate
fact: Also a honeybee alarm pheromone. A bee that stings releases it, marking you as a target for the rest of the hive.

name: Bis(2-methyl-3-furyl) disulfide
fact: One of the most intense meat odorants known, and a staple of vegetarian beef flavourings.

name: Guaiacol
fact: The core of the campfire smell. It comes from lignin breaking down as wood burns, which is why almost all smoke smells related.

name: 4-Ethylguaiacol
fact: In small amounts it reads as smoky complexity in wine; a little more and tasters start calling it band-aid or barnyard.

name: 4-Vinylguaiacol
fact: The clove note in a Bavarian wheat beer is this compound, produced by the yeast rather than by any spice.

name: Creosol
fact: A large part of what makes a peated Islay whisky smell like a bonfire on a beach.

name: Syringol
fact: Hardwood lignin produces syringol; softwood produces mostly guaiacol. It is why oak smoke and pine smoke smell different.

name: Thymol
fact: Listerine was built around thymol. Its antiseptic smell is not a coincidence. It genuinely is an antiseptic.

name: Carvacrol
fact: The smell most people file under pizza is largely carvacrol from dried oregano.

name: Menthol
fact: Menthol does not lower temperature. It binds the TRPM8 receptor that reports cold, so your nerves report a chill that is not there.

name: (R)-(−)-Carvone
fact: Identical to its mirror image in every 2D structural sense, and it smells unmistakably of spearmint while the mirror smells of caraway.

name: (S)-(+)-Carvone
fact: The exact mirror image of the spearmint molecule, and it smells of caraway instead. Your olfactory receptors are themselves chiral, so they can tell left from right.

name: Menthone
fact: Drier and less sweet than menthol, and without the cooling trick. It smells of mint but does not feel cold.

name: Pulegone
fact: Sharp and slightly medicinal. The note that makes cheap mint flavourings smell harsh.

name: Eucalyptol
fact: Also called 1,8-cineole. It is what makes a blocked nose feel briefly open. The sensation is nerve signalling, not actual airflow.

name: Camphor
fact: The smell of a grandmother's linen closet in much of the world, where camphor blocks were the standard moth repellent.

name: Borneol
fact: Camphor's alcohol counterpart. Softer, earthier, and a fixture of temple incense.

name: α-Pinene
fact: The dominant volatile in coniferous forest air, and a measurable contributor to the haze over pine-covered mountains.

name: β-Pinene
fact: Drier and less sharp than α-pinene. Together the two are most of what people mean by the smell of a Christmas tree.

name: β-Myrcene
fact: The single most abundant terpene in hops, and a large part of why an IPA smells resinous.

name: p-Cymene
fact: Forms when other terpenes oxidise, which is why an old bottle of lemon oil starts to smell dusty and turpentine-like.

name: β-Caryophyllene
fact: The only common scent molecule that also binds a cannabinoid receptor, a smell that is, technically, a drug.

name: Geraniol
fact: Honeybees release geraniol to mark flowers worth visiting and to help nestmates find the hive entrance.

name: Nerol
fact: Geraniol's cis isomer, same atoms, one bond flipped, and the result is fresher and less sweet.

name: Citronellol
fact: Pleasant to us and repellent to mosquitoes, which is the entire premise of the citronella candle.

name: Citral
fact: The definitive lemon note. Cats find it aversive, which is why citrus sprays are sold as deterrents.

name: α-Terpineol
fact: Simultaneously lilac and pine-cleaner, which is roughly the smell of a freshly mopped floor.

name: Linalyl acetate
fact: With linalool, it is what makes lavender smell like lavender rather than like generic flowers.

name: Nerolidol
fact: A quiet molecule that mostly does structural work. It holds other floral notes in place rather than announcing itself.

name: Farnesol
fact: Used in perfumery to soften and round out florals, and doubles as a signalling molecule in fungi.

name: 2-Phenylethanol
fact: The single largest component of rose oil by weight, and also a yeast by-product, which is why rising dough has a faintly floral edge.

name: Phenylacetaldehyde
fact: The green, almost metallic edge on hyacinth and narcissus that stops them smelling merely sweet.

name: β-Ionone
fact: It saturates its own receptor almost instantly, so violets seem to vanish and reappear as you smell them. The flower is not fading; you are.

name: α-Ionone
fact: Softer and more powdery than β-ionone. Closer to the smell of face powder and old cosmetics.

name: cis-Jasmone
fact: Plants nearby that detect it start ramping up their own defences, one of the clearest cases of plants using smell to talk.

name: Methyl jasmonate
fact: A plant stress hormone that travels through air. A wounded plant emits it and its neighbours pre-emptively arm themselves.

name: Hedione
fact: Introduced commercially in 1966 and now in a huge share of fine fragrance. It reads as transparency more than as a smell.

name: Benzyl acetate
fact: The most-used jasmine substitute in soap and detergent, where the real material would be prohibitively expensive.

name: Methyl anthranilate
fact: Artificial grape flavour does not smell like table grapes because it is built on Concord grapes, and this is their signature.

name: Anethole
fact: Thirteen times sweeter than sugar to the tongue, and the reason pastis turns cloudy when water is added.

name: Estragole
fact: The anise edge in fresh basil. The thing that makes basil taste of more than just green.

name: Cinnamaldehyde
fact: Cinnamon's warmth is not a metaphor. Cinnamaldehyde activates the same TRPA1 channel that reports irritation and heat.

name: Isoeugenol
fact: Most industrial vanillin was once made from isoeugenol out of clove oil, before the process moved to wood pulp.

name: Safrole
fact: Root beer tasted different before 1960, when sassafras oil was banned from food and the recipe had to be rebuilt without it.

name: Piperonal
fact: Known as heliotropin. It smells of cherry, almond and vanilla at once, which is roughly the smell of a Play-Doh tub.

name: Benzaldehyde
fact: Released alongside cyanide when amygdalin in a crushed almond breaks down. The marzipan smell is a warning label.

name: Coumarin
fact: The smell of drying hay. It is also a precursor to warfarin. Spoiled sweet clover killed cattle before anyone worked out why.

name: Methyl salicylate
fact: In North America it reads as sweets and root beer; in Britain it mostly reads as liniment. Same molecule, different childhood.

name: Raspberry ketone
fact: One of the most expensive natural flavour compounds to extract, roughly a kilogram of raspberries yields a few milligrams.

name: Zingerone
fact: Forms when raw ginger is cooked, which is why gingerbread smells sweet and warm rather than sharp like fresh root.

name: Sotolon
fact: In 2005 a maple-syrup smell repeatedly blanketed Manhattan. The source was a New Jersey plant processing fenugreek seed.

name: Abhexon
fact: Sotolon's ethyl relative, less maple, more stock cube.

name: Maltol
fact: Makes things taste sweeter without being sweet itself, so it is added to reduced-sugar products as a kind of olfactory illusion.

name: Ethyl maltol
fact: Does not occur in nature at all. It is the smell most people would call candy floss, and it was invented.

name: Cyclotene
fact: Works with sotolon to build the maple accord, and adds the burnt-sugar edge to dark roast coffee.

name: Furfural
fact: Produced whenever sugars in plant material are heated, which makes it one of the most common markers of anything cooked.

name: 5-Methylfurfural
fact: One of the compounds that separates the smell of caramel from the smell of plain sugar.

name: 2-Pentylfuran
fact: A marker of fat oxidation. The beany, cardboard note in oil that has been sitting too long.

name: 2-Acetylpyrazine
fact: One of the Maillard reaction's signature products, formed only once a surface is hot enough to brown.

name: 2,5-Dimethylpyrazine
fact: Common to almost everything browned. If a food smells toasted, some pyrazine is doing the work.

name: 2-Ethyl-3,5-dimethylpyrazine
fact: One of the most powerful roast odorants in coffee, detectable well below a part per billion.

name: 2-Acetylpyrrole
fact: Adds the faintly musty, biscuity depth underneath fresher bread notes.

name: 2-Acetylthiazole
fact: A sulfur-bearing cousin of the popcorn molecule, contributing the savoury edge to toasted grain.

name: 2-Furfurylthiol
fact: The smell of coffee the moment the bag opens. It degrades within hours, which is why fresh coffee smells so much better than old.

name: Methional
fact: The smell of a boiled potato, near-singlehandedly. Remove it and potatoes smell of almost nothing.

name: Dimethyl sulfide
fact: The smell of the sea is mostly phytoplankton breaking down. Seabirds navigate by it, tracking it to find food.

name: Dimethyl disulfide
fact: Carrion flowers emit it to imitate rotting flesh and recruit flies instead of bees.

name: Dimethyl trisulfide
fact: One of the first volatiles released by decomposing bodies. In parts per trillion it reads instead as savoury depth in cooked onion.

name: Methanethiol
fact: A major component of halitosis, and produced in your own gut. Also used to give odorless natural gas its warning smell.

name: Allicin
fact: Does not exist in an intact garlic clove. Cutting one triggers an enzyme that makes it within seconds. The smell is a defence being deployed.

name: Diallyl disulfide
fact: Passes into the bloodstream and out through the lungs, which is why garlic breath survives brushing your teeth.

name: syn-Propanethial S-oxide
fact: The onion lachrymator. It forms only when an onion is cut, drifts up, and reacts with the water film on your eye to make sulfuric acid.

name: 4-Mercapto-4-methylpentan-2-one
fact: Called cat ketone in the trade. Above threshold it smells like a litter tray; below it, like blackcurrant and boxwood.

name: 3-Mercaptohexan-1-ol
fact: The passionfruit note in a New Zealand Sauvignon is a thiol, chemically closer to skunk than to fruit.

name: Grapefruit mercaptan
fact: Among the most powerful odorants ever measured. A few tenths of a gram would scent an Olympic swimming pool.

name: 2-Butene-1-thiol
fact: A main component of skunk spray. The same class of compound forms when light hits hops in a clear beer bottle.

name: Benzothiazole
fact: The smell of a new tyre shop, and simultaneously a trace flavour compound in roasted coffee.

name: 1-Octen-3-ol
fact: Called mushroom alcohol, and also present in human breath and sweat. Mosquitoes use it to find us.

name: 1-Octen-3-one
fact: Metal has no smell. What you smell handling a coin is your own skin oils breaking down on iron, largely into this.

name: Hexanal
fact: A reliable marker of fat going rancid. The cardboard note in an old packet of crisps.

name: (E)-2-Hexenal
fact: Called leaf aldehyde. The bitter green bite in good extra-virgin olive oil is largely this.

name: (E)-2-Nonenal
fact: Rises measurably in human skin after about age forty. In Japan the resulting smell has its own word: kareishū.

name: (E,E)-2,4-Decadienal
fact: The smell of a fryer. It is the single most important compound in what people recognise as fried food.

name: Nonanal
fact: One of the aldehydes that gives clean-laundry fragrances their particular squeaky brightness.

name: Decanal
fact: Part of the aldehyde accord that made Chanel No. 5 sound like nothing else in 1921.

name: Octanal
fact: One of the compounds that makes fresh orange juice smell different from concentrate. It disappears with processing.

name: 3-Methylbutanal
fact: A Strecker degradation product. Evidence that amino acids have been heated with sugar.

name: 2-Methylbutanal
fact: Together with its isomer it forms much of the smell of chocolate that has been properly conched.

name: Isovaleric acid
fact: Foot odor and mature cheese converge here, both are the same bacteria doing the same thing to the same fatty acids.

name: Butyric acid
fact: The smell of vomit, and simultaneously an essential note in Parmesan. Context decides everything.

name: Hexanoic acid
fact: Named for goats. Caproic acid, from the Latin caper. It is largely why goat cheese smells like goats.

name: Acetic acid
fact: The simplest smell most people can name instantly, and the second-simplest carboxylic acid there is.

name: Ethyl butyrate
fact: Added back into orange juice after pasteurisation strips it out, so the carton smells like the fruit again.

name: Ethyl hexanoate
fact: One of the esters that makes a young white wine smell of fruit that is not in the bottle.

name: Ethyl 2-methylbutyrate
fact: The single most apple-smelling compound in an apple, and detectable at fractions of a part per billion.

name: Hexyl acetate
fact: Green and fruity at once. The smell of biting through the skin rather than the flesh.

name: (Z)-3-Hexenyl acetate
fact: Cut grass with a fruity edge. Predatory insects use it to locate plants currently being eaten by prey.

name: γ-Decalactone
fact: The definitive peach compound. The reason peach flavourings smell slightly creamy rather than simply fruity.

name: γ-Nonalactone
fact: Marketed for decades as aldehyde C-18 despite not being an aldehyde. It is the smell most people file under holiday.

name: δ-Decalactone
fact: The lactone that makes dairy smell rich rather than merely fatty.

name: Massoia lactone
fact: Intensely creamy at low levels and skin-irritating at high ones, so its use is tightly capped.

name: Pentadecanolide
fact: A macrocyclic musk. Sensitivity to it varies enormously between people, some cannot smell it at all.

name: Muscone
fact: The original musk, once harvested from musk deer. It is now made synthetically, which is why the deer still exist.

name: Civetone
fact: Foul at full strength and warmly skin-like when diluted a thousandfold. Perfumery is largely the art of that difference.

name: Androstenone
fact: Roughly a third of people smell urine, a third smell something sweet and floral, and a third smell nothing at all, a single gene decides which.

name: Trimethylamine
fact: Fresh fish does not smell fishy. Trimethylamine builds up only as bacteria break the flesh down, so the fish smell is a clock.

name: Cadaverine
fact: Named for exactly what you would guess. It and putrescine are the two compounds most associated with decay.

name: Putrescine
fact: Produced by your own body in small amounts, where it is essential to cell growth. The name is unhelpfully absolute.

name: p-Cresol
fact: The horse-stable note. Used in trace amounts in perfumery to give jasmine and narcissus an animal warmth.

name: Phenol
fact: Lister's original surgical antiseptic. Its smell is still the shorthand for hospital in most people's memory.

name: 4-Ethylphenol
fact: The classic barnyard fault in red wine. A little is described as complexity; more of it and the bottle is written off.

name: Acetophenone
fact: Sweet and almondy but with a hard plastic edge. The smell of a cheap cherry sweet.

name: Anisaldehyde
fact: Sits between anise and vanilla, and is used to round both out.

name: Cuminaldehyde
fact: Cumin's characteristic sweaty edge is not an accident of cooking. It is in the seed.

name: β-Damascone
fact: Fruitier and drier than damascenone. It is what gives pipe tobacco its plummy sweetness.

name: Nootkatone
fact: The bitter-woody backbone of grapefruit, and effective enough as an insect repellent to have been developed against ticks.

name: Cyclamen aldehyde
fact: Does not occur in cyclamen, or anywhere in nature. It was named after the flower it was invented to imitate.

name: Lilial
fact: For decades the default clean-laundry floral, until it was restricted in the EU in 2022 and had to be designed out of thousands of products.

name: Calone
fact: Invented in 1966, ignored for twenty years, then defined the smell of the entire 1990s. Almost every ocean-scented product traces back to it.

name: Dihydromyrcenol
fact: The smell of the entire men's fragrance aisle since 1988. Sharp, clean, faintly metallic citrus.

name: Isoamyl alcohol
fact: The main fusel alcohol in most fermentation, and a large part of why a brewery smells like a brewery.

name: Ethyl acetate
fact: Fruity in trace amounts and unmistakably solvent above them. In wine it is the first sign of spoilage.

name: 2-Heptanone
fact: Honeybees use it as a marker for already-visited flowers, and it may double as a mild anaesthetic when they bite pests.

name: 2-Nonanone
fact: Part of the ketone family that makes blue cheeses smell blue rather than just old.

name: 1-Hexanol
fact: Softer than the leaf alcohols above it. The green note that lingers after grass has been cut for an hour.

name: 1-Octanol
fact: Its oil-water partition is used as the industry standard for predicting whether a molecule will cross a cell membrane.

name: Ethanol
fact: The smell of a hospital ward is mostly this, and after 2020 it became one of the most globally recognised smells alive.

name: Acetaldehyde
fact: The compound your liver makes from alcohol before it can finish the job. The hangover is largely acetaldehyde poisoning.

name: Isobutyraldehyde
fact: Grainy and slightly sharp, a supporting player in almost anything malted.

name: Butyl acetate
fact: Simultaneously the smell of a fresh apple and of a spray-paint booth, which says something about how weak our categories are.

name: Phenylethyl acetate
fact: Rose with the sharp edges filed off. Sweeter and more honeyed than phenylethanol itself.

name: Fenchone
fact: Camphor-like and slightly bitter. The medicinal undertow in absinthe.

name: Octanoic acid
fact: Along with hexanoic acid, one of the trio of goat-named fatty acids behind the smell of aged cheese.

name: Naphthalene
fact: The mothball smell. It sublimes straight from solid to gas at room temperature, which is why a mothball vanishes without ever going wet.

name: Styrene
fact: The sweet, faintly balsamic smell of a brand-new plastic appliance out of the box.

name: 2-Methylbutanoic acid
fact: Sour and sweaty on its own, and yet part of what makes a ripe strawberry smell ripe.

name: Toluene
fact: The sweet, slightly sickly top note of a freshly painted room, and one of the largest single contributors to new car interior air.

name: m-Xylene
fact: Heavier and sweeter than toluene, and the note that keeps a new interior smelling of solvent for weeks after the car leaves the factory.

name: Ethylbenzene
fact: Outgasses from seat foam and reads as faintly petrol-like, which is why a new interior can smell like a forecourt without any fuel present.

name: 2-Ethylhexanol
fact: The plasticiser alcohol behind the smell of new vinyl. If a dashboard smells of anything, a good share of it is this.
